A greeting becomes an act of safety in a world where strangers at a door can mean danger. Abraham answers in kind and moves toward food, because prophetic hospitality does not wait for credentials before feeding travellers. The smallest exchange already reveals a home trained by generosity under blessing.

phrases.translation: Then it was not long before he brought ˹them˺ a ˹fat,˺ roasted calf
phrases.explanation: A roasted calf brought without delay shows the scale and speed of Abraham hospitality. Serving meat to unexpected guests in an ancient setting is costly work, yet he treats the strangers with a feast rather than leftovers. The detail also prepares the problem, because untouched food will signal that these guests do not belong to ordinary human need. Generosity becomes the instrument by which their nature is discovered.

phrases.translation: And when he saw that their hands did not reach for the food, he became suspicious and fearful of them.
phrases.explanation: Hands not reaching toward the calf make Abraham uneasy under customs where refusing shared food could imply hostility. He conceives fear rather than anger, since unknown men inside a home may carry an unknown mission. The story pauses at table manners to show a prophet reading social evidence carefully. What looks like a small discourtesy is actually the first crack in their human appearance.

phrases.translation: They reassured ˹him˺, “Do not be afraid! We are ˹angels˺ sent ˹only˺ against the people of Lot.”
phrases.explanation: Do not fear comes with a mission limited to the people of Lot, so the angels separate Abraham household from the judgment approaching elsewhere. Their abstaining from food is explained by nature and assignment rather than insult. The verse redirects the scene from hospitality to intercession, because Abraham love for people will not rest once a city is named. Safety for his house becomes the doorway into concern for strangers.

phrases.translation: And his wife was standing by, so she laughed, then We gave her good news of ˹the birth of˺ Isaac, and, after him, Jacob
phrases.explanation: His wife standing nearby laughs, a moment commentators explained through relief, wonder, or the news about Lot, before the glad tidings turn toward her own future. Isaac promised and Jacob after him gives not only a son but a grandson in the same sentence, multiplying old age hope beyond one cradle. A household that expected endings hears a genealogy. Laughter and prophecy meet at the edge of biological impossibility.

phrases.translation: She wondered, “Oh, my! How can I have a child in this old age,
phrases.explanation: Woe to me, shall I give birth while I am an old woman uses an exclamation of astonishment rather than an accusation against God. Sarah names the facts visible to everyone in the room, age and a barren history. Her honesty gives faith a human voice that does not pretend the announcement sounds ordinary. Wonder can be a doorway into trust when it is spoken to heaven instead of used as a reason to leave.

phrases.translation: and my husband here is an old man? This is truly an astonishing thing!”
phrases.explanation: My husband is an old man completes the natural evidence from the other side of the hoped for birth. This is an astonishing thing gives the announcement its proper scale before the angels answer. Astonishment is not yet disbelief, because she has not offered an alternative theory or a mocking label. She is asking how a word from God will enter bodies whose season appears closed.

phrases.translation: They responded, “Are you astonished by Allah’s decree? May Allah’s mercy and blessings be upon you,
phrases.explanation: Do you wonder at Allah command gently relocates the astonishing thing inside a larger pattern of divine action. The angels do not provide a biological lecture. They invoke mercy and blessings already resting on the household, suggesting that past favour makes future impossibility less foreign. A family graced across a lifetime can learn to expect that heaven arithmetic uses terms beyond age and season.

phrases.translation: O people of this house. Indeed, He is Praiseworthy, All-Glorious.”
phrases.explanation: Mercy and blessings upon the people of the house widen the promise from one womb to a prophetic household. Praiseworthy and All Glorious close the exchange by naming God as deserving thanks and full of noble generosity. The child will be a gift inside a house of prayer, hospitality, and intercession. The verse turns astonishment toward praise, which is the proper direction when impossibility becomes an appointment.

phrases.translation: Then after the fear had left Abraham, and the good news had reached him,
phrases.explanation: After fear left Abraham and good news reached him, his attention turns back to the endangered people of Lot. Personal joy does not seal his ears. The sequence matters because heaven could have ended the visit at Isaac promise, yet Abraham uses safety and happiness as a position from which to plead for others. Blessing in his home becomes moral energy toward a city he does not live in.

phrases.translation: he began to plead with Us for the people of Lot
phrases.explanation: He began to dispute or plead with Us concerning Lot people in translation language that can sound bold. Early explanation understood him asking the angels and seeking delay or mercy for any believers and possible repentance in the cities. Prophetic pleading has already been limited with Noah, yet Abraham does not know where the boundary lies here. Compassion explores every lawful opening before accepting that a decree is final.

phrases.translation: Truly, Abraham was forbearing, tender-hearted, and ever turning ˹to his Lord˺
phrases.explanation: Abraham was forbearing, tenderly sighing or deeply compassionate, and constantly returning to Allah, a cluster that explains the pleading without excusing the city. Forbearing means he could hold pain without rushing to condemnation. Ever returning gives the source of his tenderness, because a heart trained by repentance knows the value of another chance. The verse pauses to honour the character inside an unsuccessful intercession.

phrases.translation: ˹The angels said,˺ “O Abraham! Plead no more! Your Lord’s decree has already come,
phrases.explanation: Turn away from this tells Abraham that pleading has reached the border set by a decree already come from his Lord. The angels are not rebuking compassion. They are closing a case after the city record and God knowledge have settled it. Abraham tenderness remains praiseworthy even where it cannot alter the outcome. A prophet can exhaust mercy in argument and still be required to submit to justice.

phrases.translation: and they will certainly be afflicted with a punishment that cannot be averted!”
phrases.explanation: A punishment not to be turned back will reach them gives finality to the errand first announced at the table. This is no longer a warning whose timing can be negotiated by a righteous relative in another town. The sentence also protects Abraham from carrying failure home with the good news of Isaac. Some outcomes sit beyond intercession, and recognising that boundary is part of trusting the Judge.

phrases.translation: When Our messenger-angels came to Lot, he was distressed and worried by their arrival.
phrases.explanation: When the messengers come to Lot he is distressed and feels his power narrow around them. He knows the habits of his city and the danger handsome guests will attract under the code of hospitality he must honour. The same visit that comforted Abraham causes local panic because setting changes the meaning of a knock. Innocent travellers become a test the town has practised failing.

phrases.translation: He said, “This is a terrible day.”
phrases.explanation: This is a hard day compresses Lot knowledge of his neighbours into one sentence. A prophet living among persistent corruption may measure time by anticipated shame rather than by hours. His distress also shows that moral clarity does not come with physical strength to enforce it. The day is hard because duty to guests and weakness before a crowd arrive at his door in the same moment.

phrases.translation: And ˹the men of˺ his people—who were used to shameful deeds—came to him rushing.
phrases.explanation: His people come rushing toward him, already habituated to shameful deeds before this night. Speed tells the reader that news of guests travels through the city as an opportunity rather than a curiosity. A public crowd approaching a prophet house has left private temptation far behind. The scene is about coercion, violation of hospitality, and a society whose desire expects no resistance from law or neighbourly shame.

phrases.translation: He pleaded, “O my people! Here are my daughters ˹for marriage˺—they are pure for you.
phrases.explanation: Here are my daughters, they are purer for you has been explained by commentators as an appeal toward lawful marriage with women of the community or in other readings his own daughters offered in marriage under desperate protection of guests. The exact application is discussed, while the moral direction is clear. Lot pleads for a lawful road and against assault, using every social language available before force reaches the door.

phrases.translation: So fear Allah, and do not humiliate me by disrespecting my guests.
phrases.explanation: Fear Allah and do not disgrace me concerning my guests joins God consciousness with the strongest local code they still claim to understand. Guest protection was a measure of honour across the ancient world, so Lot asks for restraint at two levels. Disgrace would fall on his household if visitors were seized under his roof. The crowd is being warned that their act attacks faith, manhood, custom, and the safety owed to strangers at once.

phrases.translation: Is there not ˹even˺ a single right-minded man among you?”
phrases.explanation: Is there not one right minded man among you searches the crowd for a single conscience able to slow the rush. One voice might remind neighbours of shame before the whole city becomes one body. The question is heartbreaking because Lot is not asking for an army. He is asking for ordinary maturity, the minimum social material from which repentance or restraint might have begun in that doorway.

phrases.translation: They argued, “You certainly know that we have no need for your daughters. You already know what we desire!”
phrases.explanation: You know we have no claim or desire for your daughters and you know what we want makes the crowd unusually explicit. They refuse the lawful alternative and name Lot knowledge as if shared history settles the matter. Desire has become a public policy answerable to neither God nor hospitality. The verse removes ambiguity for the reader, because the city representatives state their chosen corruption in direct speech.

phrases.translation: He responded, “If only I had the strength ˹to resist you˺ or could rely on a strong supporter.”
phrases.explanation: If only I had power against you or a strong pillar to lean on gives Lot a moment of profound human weakness. Pillar suggests clan, protectors, or physical support absent in a town where he is an outsider prophet. The wish is not unbelief. It is the sound of a man measuring a door against a crowd. Heaven answer will show that the pillar was already inside the house in a form he had not yet recognised.

phrases.translation: The angels said, “O Lot! We are the messengers of your Lord.
phrases.explanation: We are messengers of your Lord changes the balance at the door without a visible army entering the street. The guests Lot tried to protect become the agents who protect him, completing the hospitality reversal. Your Lord personalises the mission, because the God who sent judgement to the city has also kept custody of His prophet inside it. Fear begins to move from the house to the crowd.

phrases.translation: They will never reach you. So travel with your family in the dark of night,
phrases.explanation: They will never reach you promises a barrier around Lot before travel begins. Journey with your family during part of the night gives the rescue a quiet hour and a direction away from the morning appointment. Night travel suits a small household slipping beyond a city whose rulers cannot be trusted. The command combines trust with practical movement, as deliverance often does in these stories.

phrases.translation: and do not let any of you look back, except your wife.
phrases.explanation: No one should look back except your wife carries a difficult exception that early commentators read in more than one grammatical way, whether she remains, looks, or is excepted from the saved family. The outcome is clear in the next sentence. Looking back can picture attachment to the doomed city as much as physical turning. A rescue can be lost at the neck when the heart keeps facing home.

phrases.translation: She will certainly suffer the fate of the others. Their appointed time is the morning. Is the morning not near?”
phrases.explanation: What strikes them will strike her and their appointment is morning settles the family tragedy with the same painful definition learned by Noah. Marriage to a prophet cannot substitute for inward loyalty when a city falls. Is morning not near turns an ordinary approaching dawn into a sentence already walking toward the streets. Lot hardest day is about to end by a sunrise nobody in the city should welcome.

phrases.translation: When Our command came, We turned the cities upside down and rained down on them clustered stones of baked clay
phrases.explanation: When Our command came We made the highest part lowest and rained marked stones of baked clay in layers. The image of overturned cities gives physical form to a society that inverted hospitality, desire, and law. Stones in succession suggest no random single accident but a directed judgment. Traditional discussion of the Dead Sea region surrounds the passage, yet the Quran emphasis remains the moral inversion made visible in geography.

phrases.translation: marked by your Lord ˹O Prophet˺. And these stones are not far from the ˹pagan˺ wrongdoers
phrases.explanation: Marked from your Lord gives each stone an assignment in classical explanation, sometimes pictured with the name of its target. Whether read with that report or more generally as specially appointed, the marking removes chaos from the scene. Not far from wrongdoers then turns toward Muhammad audience and every later oppressor. An ancient ruin can be geographically distant while its warning sits beside a present city with similar deeds.

phrases.translation: And to the people of Midian We sent their brother Shu’aib.
phrases.explanation: To Midian their brother Shuaib brings prophecy into a trading society rather than a court or mountain fortress. Midian is associated in the stories with markets, travel routes, and inherited religion around a sacred grove in other passages. Brother again establishes local trust. A commercial people will now hear the universal sentence about worship translated immediately into scales, coins, and the rights of strangers at a stall.

phrases.translation: He said, “O my people! Worship Allah. You have no god other than Him.
phrases.explanation: Worship Allah, no god other than Him, remains first even where the famous local corruption will be economic. Market reform in this story does not begin with technique alone. It begins by removing rival gods made from profit, custom, and ancestors. When Allah is set at the centre, a measuring cup becomes a theological object because every transaction now occurs before an unseen witness.

phrases.translation: And do not give short measure and weight. I do see you in prosperity now,
phrases.explanation: Do not diminish measure and weight names the fraud by which buyers receive less than the price announces. Short changing can look small per customer while building an economy of suspicion across a region. I see you in prosperity removes poverty as an excuse, since their cheating is greed inside abundance rather than desperation. The prophet reads their present comfort as blessing at risk rather than evidence of innocence.

phrases.translation: but I truly fear for you the torment of an overwhelming Day
phrases.explanation: I fear for you the punishment of an encompassing Day turns shop practice toward final judgment and possible worldly ruin. Encompassing suggests a day from which no market stall or family vault can step outside. Fear for you again carries pastoral concern, a merchant prophet warning people whose ledgers look healthy. A few grains stolen at a scale become large when the Day weighs the hand that held it.

phrases.translation: O my people! Give full measure and weigh with justice.
phrases.explanation: Give full measure and weight with justice states the positive practice before restating the theft. Justice at a scale means the same quantity for stranger, poor buyer, political ally, and respected elder. A balance can preach before a tongue does, because customers learn whether God is feared in the pause while grain settles. Shuaib reform begins with an ordinary motion repeated hundreds of times in public.

phrases.translation: Do not defraud people of their property, nor go about spreading corruption in the land
phrases.explanation: Do not deprive people of their things widens theft beyond the moment of measurement to every quiet reduction of rights. Nor spread corruption in the earth places repeated market fraud inside social ecology, since broken trust makes travel, credit, food, and neighbourly confidence decay together. A coin clipped in one shop can teach a whole road to expect cheating. The verse refuses to call that private cleverness.

phrases.translation: What is left ˹as a lawful gain˺ by Allah is far better for you if you are ˹truly˺ believers.
phrases.explanation: What Allah leaves you is better means the lawful profit remaining after full measure is worth more than the extra slice taken by fraud. Early commentators also read the remainder of Allah as obedience and its lasting reward. A smaller honest gain can carry blessing, sleep, reputation, and a clean account. The verse gives merchants an alternative imagination in which enough lawful increase beats anxious abundance.

phrases.translation: And I am not a keeper over you.”
phrases.explanation: I am not a keeper over you limits Shuaib role to delivery and witness rather than shop police inside every conscience. A prophet can name the rule and warn about the Day while leaving the hand at the scale responsible for its next movement. That sentence protects both preacher and audience from confusing surveillance with faith. The market becomes a place where unseen God consciousness must do what inspectors cannot.

phrases.translation: They asked ˹sarcastically˺, “O Shu’aib! Does your prayer command you that we should abandon what our forefathers worshipped or give up managing our wealth as we please?
phrases.explanation: Does your prayer command you makes worship the alleged source of economic interference, a sarcastic question from traders who want religion kept away from ledgers. Ancestors and freedom with wealth stand together because inherited gods often protect inherited business methods. Managing property as we please sounds like liberty until the customers property enters the sentence. The verse captures a familiar demand that faith decorate private life while leaving profitable injustice untouched.

phrases.translation: Indeed, you are such a tolerant, sensible man!”
phrases.explanation: You are the forbearing and sensible one is read by most listeners in context as mockery, although the words can carry a surface compliment. Calling Shuaib reasonable while rejecting his reason allows the council to sound polite as it dismisses him. Sarcasm becomes a social tool for refusing reform without offering a better scale. The compliment also admits his public character, which makes their treatment of the message harder to justify.

phrases.translation: He said, “O my people! Consider if I stand on a clear proof from my Lord and He has blessed me with a good provision from Him.
phrases.explanation: Consider if I stand on clear proof and have been given good provision from Him answers suspicion that reform is envy of merchant success. Shuaib own lawful sustenance shows that a person can live without stealing measures. Clear proof gives his economic teaching a source beyond personal taste. He asks the market to judge the whole picture, including a preacher whose table does not depend on the fraud he condemns.

phrases.translation: I do not want to do what I am forbidding you from.
phrases.explanation: I do not want to oppose you by doing what I forbid you is one of the great integrity sentences of the chapter. A reformer secretly using the banned scale would convert morality into monopoly. Shuaib refuses the professional advantage of rules applied only outward. This consistency gives his words weight with ordinary shoppers who know exactly how religious language can be used to clear competitors from a profitable road.

phrases.translation: I only intend reform to the best of my ability.
phrases.explanation: I only intend reform as far as I am able states aim and limit in one breath. Reform is constructive rather than gleeful exposure, while ability prevents a prophet from promising to remake society by willpower. The sentence answers sarcasm with transparent motive. He is not trying to confiscate wealth or become market chief. He wants the relationships around wealth repaired before the Day weighs everyone at once.

phrases.translation: My success comes only through Allah. In Him I trust and to Him I turn
phrases.explanation: My success is only through Allah and to Him I trust and return places outcomes back in divine hands. A reformer can speak clearly, model honesty, and still watch a town choose fraud. Trust stops that result from turning the messenger into a manipulator willing to cheat for a holy goal. Returning repeatedly to Allah also keeps the heart soft while public conversation grows hostile.

phrases.translation: O my people! Do not let your opposition to me lead you to a fate similar to that of the people of Noah, or Hûd, or Ṣâliḥ.
phrases.explanation: Do not let opposition to me bring upon you what struck Noah, Hud, and Salih peoples names the risk that personal dislike of a messenger becomes national suicide. Shuaib separates his feelings from their future by warning them as my people even while they threaten his standing. The list turns this chapter from literature into a map of nearby endings. They are being asked to choose before becoming another recited example.

phrases.translation: And the people of Lot are not far from you
phrases.explanation: The people of Lot are not far from you can point to geography, time, or moral similarity, and early readings allowed several nearnesses to work together. Midian merchants travelling roads could know ruined places and recent memory better than a distant audience. Nearness removes the alibi that judgment belongs only to primitive strangers. A warning becomes urgent when the example can almost be visited by caravan.

phrases.translation: So seek your Lord’s forgiveness and turn to Him in repentance.
phrases.explanation: Seek forgiveness and repent repeats the invitation after irony and threats have entered the conversation. Shuaib does not let their manners decide whether mercy remains available. Fraudulent merchants can return goods, correct scales, restore rights, and begin again before the blast writes the ending. Repentance in a market has practical steps, which makes forgiveness visible in refunds and honest weights as well as private sorrow.

phrases.translation: Surely my Lord is Most Merciful, All-Loving.”
phrases.explanation: My Lord is Merciful and Loving gives the returning sinner two names to approach after economic guilt. Loving carries affection toward repentant servants, an especially tender note in a chapter filled with destroyed towns. Shuaib does not market a cold tribunal only. He presents a Lord who welcomes repaired hands. The sentence makes clear that rejecting such a God in favour of fraudulent profit is the true bad exchange.

phrases.translation: They threatened, “O Shu’aib! We do not comprehend much of what you say, and surely we see you powerless among us.
phrases.explanation: We do not understand much of what you say may express deliberate incomprehension, contempt for his style, or a claim that moral teaching sounds foreign inside their market language. We see you weak among us adds social measurement, because Shuaib lacks a force able to protect him from the majority. The verse combines intellectual dismissal with a threat assessment. Truth is being priced by the speaker bodyguard rather than by its evidence.

phrases.translation: Were it not for your clan, we would have certainly stoned you, for you are nothing to us.”
phrases.explanation: Were it not for your clan we would have stoned you reveals that clan deterrence, not conscience, is preserving his life. You are not mighty against us completes their scale of honour in one sentence. A society can sound orderly while its restraint depends entirely on retaliation. Shuaib weakness in their eyes becomes the setting for his next question, where he compares reverence for a family network with reverence for God.

phrases.translation: He said, “O my people! Do you have more regard for my clan than for Allah, turning your back on Him entirely?
phrases.explanation: Is my clan mightier in your sight than Allah exposes a ranking they may not have intended to say aloud. They hesitate before human relatives while openly disobeying the Lord, turning their backs on Him as a discarded object in the image of the verse. Social fear has become their functional theology. The question is devastating because it uses their own threat to draw the map of what they actually respect.

phrases.translation: Surely my Lord is Fully Aware of what you do
phrases.explanation: My Lord encompasses what you do makes the market, council, clan calculation, and threat sit inside divine knowledge. Encompassing is stronger than merely hearing about acts later, since no deed can move outside the circle to become invisible. The same word has framed the encompassing Day feared by Shuaib. A God around every action cannot be managed by turning a back, which is why the posture in the previous sentence looks so futile.

phrases.translation: O my people! Persist in your ways, for I ˹too˺ will persist in mine.
phrases.explanation: Work according to your position and I am working gives both sides their chosen direction after argument has reached a wall. Position can mean place, condition, or method, and the sentence allows the town to reveal itself through continued action. Shuaib does not answer a stoning threat with a rival militia. He announces a moral race toward an outcome God will judge, a form of confidence that needs no immediate audience victory.

phrases.translation: You will soon come to know who will be visited by a humiliating torment and is a liar!
phrases.explanation: You will know who receives humiliating punishment and who the liar is turns their lying accusation into a future public test. In a commercial town, liars are usually exposed by scales and contracts, yet this ultimate test will measure prophetic claims. The sentence is not personal revenge. It hands the contested labels to an event that neither party can edit afterward, making time itself a witness against propaganda.

phrases.translation: And watch! I too am watching with you!”
phrases.explanation: Watch and I am watching with you creates an uneasy shared lookout over the approaching result. Waiting has been the posture of prophets across the chapter, from Noah at the Ark to Muhammad hearing these stories. Opponents wait for the preacher to fade, while the preacher waits for heaven word to ripen. The final clause gives patience an active sound, since attention itself becomes obedience when no further argument will be heard.

phrases.translation: When Our command came, We saved Shu’aib and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us.
phrases.explanation: When Our command came Shuaib and believers were saved by mercy, continuing the rescue grammar of the chapter. A marketplace minority can be extracted from a town whose economy felt indispensable to everyone living in it. Mercy means their honest scales were not a magical shield owned by them. God separates people by response to truth when public success finally stops deciding who looks safe.

phrases.translation: And the ˹mighty˺ blast overtook the wrongdoers, so they fell lifeless in their homes
phrases.explanation: The mighty blast seized wrongdoers and morning found them lifeless in their homes, repeating the Thamud ending in a trading town. Houses filled through cheating become silent showrooms of interrupted accounts. A sound that nobody can bargain with ends negotiations more completely than an argument could. The repetition teaches Muhammad audience to see a pattern rather than isolated disasters, because the moral causes rhyme across different civilisations.

phrases.translation: as if they had never lived there. So away with Midian as it was with Thamûd
phrases.explanation: As if they had never lived there and away with Midian as Thamud was distanced makes comparison part of the epitaph. Traders and stone carvers now share the same grammar of absence. Their local sins differed in texture, yet rejection after a brother messenger brought a common end. The verse encourages readers not to overvalue the surface of a culture when judging spiritual danger. Different roads can arrive at the same empty street.

phrases.translation: Indeed, We sent Moses with Our signs and compelling proof
phrases.explanation: Moses sent with signs and manifest authority compresses a long mission into one line after several Arabian stories. Authority suggests proof strong enough to confront a state rather than private inspiration alone. By changing scale from towns and markets to Pharaoh court, the chapter widens its warning. A messenger can face families, merchants, builders, or empire and still meet the same protected refusal wearing more expensive clothing.

phrases.translation: to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they followed the command of Pharaoh, and Pharaoh’s command was not well guided
phrases.explanation: They followed Pharaoh command although his command was not rightly guided diagnoses leadership as a shared moral act. Pharaoh issues the order, yet chiefs and people lend it bodies, labour, silence, and applause. Not rightly guided is an understated sentence with enormous reach, because a whole administration can become efficient at walking the wrong road. The verse refuses to let followers hide entirely inside a famous tyrant biography.

phrases.translation: He will be before his people on the Day of Judgment and will lead them into the Fire.
phrases.explanation: He will go before his people on the Day of Resurrection and lead them down to the Fire makes leadership continue past death as procession. The verb of leading to water turns bitter, since a guide who once promised provision and glory brings his followers to a burning drink. Political loyalty therefore has an afterlife. People are asked to imagine the front of the parade before joining the comfort of its middle.

phrases.translation: What an evil place to be led into
phrases.explanation: Evil is the place of arrival or watering place evaluates the destination after the procession has been pictured. A landing place should mean relief after travel, yet this one multiplies horror. The sentence is brief because no further decoration is needed once the road ends in Fire. It also answers every tyrant public language about progress, since a movement is finally known by where its followers are made to stand.

phrases.translation: They were followed by a curse in this ˹life˺ and ˹will receive another˺ on the Day of Judgment. What an evil gift to receive
phrases.explanation: A curse follows them here and on Resurrection Day while the gift given is called evil, joining reputation and destiny in one bitter package. A gift normally honours a guest, so the word carries the same ironic reversal as leading people to water that burns. Pharaoh party receive the return prepared by their chosen command. History remembers them with condemnation, and the future receives them without the palace that once filtered every entrance.

phrases.translation: These are accounts, We relate to you ˹O Prophet˺, of the ˹destroyed˺ cities.
phrases.explanation: These are reports of towns related to the Prophet marks a deliberate pause after the procession of nations. Reports rather than legends is the claim carried by the passage voice, with geography and ruins available to hearers. The storyteller is God addressing Muhammad, which ties ancient settlements to a present messenger under pressure. Each town has functioned as evidence and comfort without needing to become a long independent history book.

phrases.translation: Some are still standing ˹barren˺, while others have been mowed down
phrases.explanation: Some standing and some mowed down uses harvest language for settlements, with walls or traces remaining in one place and complete disappearance in another. Travellers might pass a visible ruin on one journey and hear only a name on the next. Both forms teach, because a standing empty house and a levelled field say that human permanence has degrees of evidence but no exemption. The land itself becomes an archive.

phrases.translation: We did not wrong them, rather they wronged themselves. The gods they invoked beside Allah were of no help at all when the command of your Lord came, and only contributed to their ruin
phrases.explanation: We did not wrong them but they wronged themselves gathers every destroyed town under the fairness principle of the chapter. Their gods gave no help when the command arrived and only increased ruin by occupying trust that might have turned to God. A false helper can damage twice, first by promising rescue and then by consuming the time in which real rescue was sought. Self wronging includes choosing furniture as a lifeboat.

phrases.translation: Such is the ˹crushing˺ grip of your Lord when He seizes the societies entrenched in wrongdoing.
phrases.explanation: Such is the seizure of your Lord when He seizes towns in wrongdoing uses the accumulated stories as a definition rather than isolated accidents. Gripping suggests a hold from which local strength, beauty, armies, markets, and cliffs cannot wriggle free. Towns are seized as social bodies after public injustice hardens into a system. The verse speaks slowly because the reader has just walked through enough streets to recognise the hand.

phrases.translation: Indeed, His grip is ˹terribly˺ painful and severe
phrases.explanation: His seizure is painful and severe closes the definition without a rescue clause for spectators. Severity belongs to the moral scale of societies that had prophets, signs, warnings, prosperity, and time. This is not a licence to call every disaster a known judgment on its victims. In the chapter, scenes are interpreted by revelation. The lesson for readers is humility before a God whose patience should never be mistaken for absence.

phrases.translation: Surely in this is a sign for those who fear the torment of the Hereafter.
phrases.explanation: In this is a sign for one who fears punishment of the Hereafter tells readers how to use ruins. Earthly seizure becomes a sample and pointer rather than the whole sentence, because death in a town judgment still leads to a greater gathering. Fear that reads signs is productive, unlike curiosity that collects photographs of disaster. The verse turns the eyes from old stones to a future court where the same people must stand again.

phrases.translation: That is a Day for which humanity will be gathered and a Day ˹that will be˺ witnessed ˹by all˺
phrases.explanation: That Day is one for which people are gathered and a Day witnessed expands the audience beyond any town or generation. Witnessed can embrace angels, prophets, peoples, and the whole courtly scene of judgment in early explanation. No one can schedule a private hearing or rely on being forgotten in an unmarked settlement. Public history inside the Quran is preparing readers for a far more public day when local memory no longer controls who gets heard.

phrases.translation: We only delay it for a fixed term
phrases.explanation: We only delay it for a counted term sets the vast gathering inside an exact but undisclosed limit. Counted removes randomness while preserving human ignorance of the number. Every generation that calls delay evidence against judgment is standing inside the count it doubts. The short verse bears enormous weight because it explains the silence between warning and arrival without surrendering the certainty of arrival.

phrases.translation: When that Day arrives, no one will dare speak except with His permission.
phrases.explanation: On the Day it comes no soul speaks except by permission changes the sound of the universe after chapters filled with argument. Chieftains, merchants, tyrants, crowds, and prophets who debated in towns will discover that speech itself needs authority. Intercession and testimony remain possible only inside permission. The silence first teaches scale, because a court where even a sentence waits for leave cannot be managed by reputation.

phrases.translation: Some of them will be miserable, others joyful
phrases.explanation: Some miserable and some happy divides the gathered world by final condition rather than by town, ancestry, profession, or architectural style. The simple pair gathers Noah son, Pharaoh, merchants, poor believers, and unborn readers into two companies. Earthly labels have not disappeared from the record, but they no longer organise the seating. The verse asks which of the two words a present life is slowly learning to answer to.

phrases.translation: As for those bound for misery, they will be in the Fire, where they will be sighing and gasping
phrases.explanation: The miserable in the Fire have sighing and exhaling, sounds of distress often pictured in early commentary as the harsh breathing of a donkey or a chest labouring under pain. The detail is auditory because hell is imagined not only as a place seen but as an environment of groaning. Breath itself becomes suffering rather than relief. After speech required permission, even involuntary sound tells the condition of the speaker.

phrases.translation: staying there forever, as long as the heavens and the earth will endure, except what your Lord wills.
phrases.explanation: Remaining there as long as heavens and earth endure uses the largest familiar durations to express permanence in the world to come. Early commentators discussed heavens and earth of the Hereafter and the exception by God will, with several interpretations concerning entry, delay, or people later removed. The wording should not be flattened by choosing one detail too quickly. Its clear force in context is a stay no human timetable can outlast.

phrases.translation: Surely your Lord does what He intends
phrases.explanation: Your Lord does what He wills protects divine freedom around the exception and prevents readers from turning eternity into a mechanism outside God. Will in this setting is wise and just rather than arbitrary mood, consistent with the chapter insistence that nobody is wronged. The sentence may humble theological curiosity at exactly the point where systems want a complete map. Final outcomes remain under the Lord whose record and mercy are both exact.

phrases.translation: And as for those destined to joy, they will be in Paradise,
phrases.explanation: The happy in Paradise mirrors the miserable company with the destination of guided lives. Happiness here is not a brief mood after relief, which the chapter earlier exposed as unstable. It is a settled state inside a place prepared for people whose patience and good deeds were recorded through changing fortune. The parallel structure gives joy solidity, because the same sentence shape that imprisoned others now opens a garden.

phrases.translation: staying there forever, as long as the heavens and the earth will endure,
phrases.explanation: Remaining as long as heavens and earth endure gives Paradise a duration beyond the cycles that cut down crops, towns, and bodies. Readers who have watched settlements mowed down need a home no season can harvest. The figure uses cosmic scale to train desire away from brief enjoyment. Permanence is part of the reward because love, worship, food, companionship, and safety no longer have to race an approaching end.

phrases.translation: except what your Lord wills—a ˹generous˺ giving, without end
phrases.explanation: Except what your Lord wills followed by a gift not cut off resolves the exception in favour of unbroken favour for the people of Paradise in the dominant reading. Early discussion explored stages before entry and the beginning of the stay, while uninterrupted gift protects the promise from anxiety. Imagine every good thing in the chapter that was withdrawn, mocked, drowned, or blasted. Here giving itself is the thing that will not be interrupted.

phrases.translation: So do not be in doubt ˹O Prophet˺ about what those ˹pagans˺ worship.
phrases.explanation: Do not be in doubt about what these people worship returns the Prophet to Mecca after universal judgment. The present idols may look socially alive, yet their nature has already been settled by every absent partner in the stories. Doubt here would mean letting crowds create uncertainty after evidence has accumulated. The verse gives a preacher stability when the local version of an old falsehood seems newly confident.

phrases.translation: They worship nothing except what their forefathers worshipped before ˹them˺.
phrases.explanation: They only worship as their fathers worshipped before identifies inheritance as the operating system of current denial. A father practice can feel like knowledge merely because it arrives with childhood language and family honour. The sentence strips novelty from their defence, since Thamud had already used ancestors as a shield. Muhammad audience is therefore not facing a unique argument that needs a unique surrender from him.

phrases.translation: And We will certainly give them their share ˹of punishment˺ in full, without any reduction
phrases.explanation: We will pay them their portion in full without decrease answers portion language used for worldly enjoyment earlier. Just as deeds aimed only at earth were paid without reduction, punishment for persistent association will not be discounted by ancestry or number. Fullness cuts in both directions under divine justice. Nobody receives less mercy than promised and nobody escapes through a clerical error in the record.

phrases.translation: Indeed, We had given Moses the Scripture, but differences arose regarding it.
phrases.explanation: Moses was given the Book and disagreement arose concerning it, bringing the discussion to a scripture community closer to Muhammad setting. Possession of revelation does not by itself guarantee unified reception, since interpretation, rivalry, and rejection can grow around a genuine gift. This prepares the Prophet for disagreement over the Quran without making disagreement evidence against its source. A Book can be clear and still meet divided readers.

phrases.translation: Had it not been for a prior decree from your Lord, their differences would have been settled ˹at once˺.
phrases.explanation: Had it not been for a word already gone forth judgment between disputants would have been settled immediately. The prior word is the appointed delay until resurrection, the same counted term running under the chapter. Postponement allows individuals to move, repent, inherit arguments, and reveal motives over time. It also restrains the impatient wish of believers to force every religious dispute into a visible verdict before its hour.

phrases.translation: They are truly in alarming doubt about it
phrases.explanation: They are in disquieting doubt about it repeats the phrase used by Thamud people, linking scriptural dispute to an ancient emotional state. Doubt that agitates can become research, yet it can also become permanent suspicion used to avoid surrender. The verse does not require the Prophet to solve every interior weather pattern among readers of earlier Books. It teaches him that revealed words have always met hearts at different levels of rest.

phrases.translation: And surely your Lord will fully pay all for their deeds.
phrases.explanation: Your Lord will fully repay everyone for their deeds gathers disputants, believers, town destroyers, and quiet worshippers into one exact payroll. Full repayment answers both fears, namely that hidden good will be lost and hidden wrong will be excused by crowd membership. The verse bridges argument over Books with final conduct. What a person did with the truth received becomes more important than which inherited banner surrounded the doing.

phrases.translation: He is certainly All-Aware of what they do
phrases.explanation: He is aware of what they do makes full repayment possible without error or dependence on public dossiers. Awareness includes motive, capacity, knowledge, coercion, and persistence, distinctions human parties flatten during religious conflict. This knowledge allows delay to continue safely until the appointed settling. For the Prophet it is also relief, because he does not need to become the final accountant of every disputant through history.

phrases.translation: So be steadfast as you are commanded ˹O Prophet˺, along with those who turn ˹in submission to Allah˺ with you.
phrases.explanation: Remain steadfast as you are commanded is the personal command distilled from all the prophet stories. Popularly remembered as a weighty instruction, it asks for straightness in worship, delivery, patience, and character without bending toward audience edits. Those who repent with him are included because steadfastness is communal work, not a private pose. A leader straightens a road partly by walking it where followers can see.

phrases.translation: And do not transgress. Surely He is All-Seeing of what you ˹believers˺ do
phrases.explanation: Do not transgress adds restraint to steadfastness so zeal does not become excess, cruelty, invention, or despairing violence. He sees what you do gives the command a watcher whose sight is encouragement and boundary at once. The verse sits after destroyed towns because responding communities can also go wrong while trying to avoid the old errors. Straightness means neither softening truth for the council nor overshooting it in anger.

phrases.translation: And do not be inclined to the wrongdoers or you will be touched by the Fire.
phrases.explanation: Do not incline toward wrongdoers warns against leaning into their approval, alliance, protection, or moral direction until their path begins to feel normal. Inclination can start as manners, funding, silence, or admiration for efficiency. The Fire touching the one who leans makes small angles matter, because a road is chosen by repeated degrees before a person notices the destination. Steadfastness therefore needs social vigilance as well as private belief.

phrases.translation: For then you would have no protectors other than Allah, nor would you be helped
phrases.explanation: No protectors besides Allah and no help then exposes the destination of leaning on the wrong pillars. The wrongdoers who looked like shelter in a hostile town cannot protect a soul at the court. Help language returns to Noah search for support and Hud trust under threat. A believer may need neighbours, agreements, and ordinary alliances, yet ultimate leaning must remain where final protection exists.

phrases.translation: Establish prayer ˹O Prophet˺ at both ends of the day and in the early part of the night.
phrases.explanation: Establish prayer at the two ends of the day and in approaches of the night gives steadfastness a daily timetable. Early commentators mapped these times onto the obligatory prayers in detailed ways, while the verse itself frames morning, evening, and night with remembrance. A person resisting wrongdoing needs repeated returns to God before public pressure shapes the inner angle. Prayer becomes maintenance for a straight road rather than decoration after moral decisions.

phrases.translation: Surely good deeds wipe out evil deeds. That is a reminder for the mindful
phrases.explanation: Good deeds wipe out evil deeds offers repair inside the same day rather than leaving a person frozen by the last failure. Prayers and righteous acts can erase traces through Allah forgiveness, especially when joined to repentance and restored rights where people were harmed. A reminder for those who remember means this mercy works on hearts willing to return. The verse gives ordinary believers a practical rhythm after the cosmic scale of towns and eternity.

phrases.translation: And be patient! Certainly Allah does not discount the reward of the good-doers
phrases.explanation: Be patient and Allah does not waste the reward of good doers returns the command given to the Prophet at the end of Noah story. Patience here includes prayer, refusal to incline, and endurance when reform seems slower than mockery. Not wasting reward answers the fear that quiet faithfulness disappears beside famous prophetic rescues. Every hidden act of excellence remains in an account managed by a Lord who loses nothing entrusted to Him.

phrases.translation: If only there had been among the ˹destroyed˺ peoples before you,
phrases.explanation: Why were there not among earlier generations people of remaining virtue who forbade corruption asks a searching question over the ruined archive. A remnant of morally serious people might have restrained markets, councils, crowds, and courts before judgment became the only language left. The verse does not deny that messengers came. It asks why so few citizens joined the work of public correction once truth was available.

phrases.translation: ˹O believers,˺ virtuous individuals who forbade corruption in the land—
phrases.explanation: Virtuous individuals forbidding corruption in the land describes a social function wider than personal piety. Corruption grows when honest people treat public harm as someone else department, leaving merchants, tyrants, and mobs to set the weather. A few saved people are excepted because small believing remnants did exist. Their scarcity is the indictment of the majority, not proof that reform required a population no town could produce.

phrases.translation: other than the few We had saved ˹from the torment˺.
phrases.explanation: Other than the few We saved keeps the exception visible before the majority pattern is named. Noah company, Hud believers, Salih followers, Lot household in part, and Shuaib people show that rescue found a remnant each time. Fewness should therefore produce humility rather than contempt for small groups doing right. A society may be judged by the corrupt many while its future hope is carried by an almost invisible minority.

phrases.translation: But the wrongdoers ˹only˺ pursued their ˹worldly˺ pleasures, becoming wicked
phrases.explanation: Wrongdoers pursued the luxury in which they lived and were guilty identifies comfort as a sedative that kept them from forbidding corruption. Luxury itself can be lawful, yet pursuit of it as the main project makes public conscience feel expensive. They followed ease through towns that needed interruption. The verse explains the silence before destruction as a lifestyle, because people protecting a soft life rarely volunteer to become unpopular.

phrases.translation: And your Lord ˹O Prophet˺ would never destroy a society unjustly while its people were acting rightly
phrases.explanation: Your Lord would not destroy towns unjustly while their people were reformers states the moral safeguard after lamenting how few reformers stood up. A society actively repairing corruption, belief, and relationships is not swept away under a careless decree. Early readings also stressed that Allah does not punish a town for association alone while its people treat one another justly, a discussion best held carefully. The central assurance remains divine justice joined to social responsibility.

phrases.translation: Had your Lord so willed, He would have certainly made humanity one single community ˹of believers˺, but they will always ˹choose to˺ differ—
phrases.explanation: Had your Lord willed He would have made humanity one community places continuing difference inside a world designed for testing rather than mechanical unity. They will not cease to differ predicts argument across religion, provision, and obedience as far as human history runs. The verse prevents believers from treating disagreement itself as proof that revelation failed. Uniform belief by compulsion was possible for divine power, yet responsibility and mercy unfold through chosen response.

phrases.translation: except those shown mercy by your Lord—and so He created them ˹to choose freely˺.
phrases.explanation: Except those your Lord has mercy on identifies a company held in agreement on truth and guided through difference without being consumed by it. For that He created them has been read in relation to mercy, difference, or the whole testing pattern, and commentators discussed the referent carefully. The verse should therefore not be used as a blunt slogan about why individuals exist. It places creation, choice, mercy, and dispute inside a wisdom larger than a single sentence can flatten.

phrases.translation: And so the Word of your Lord will be fulfilled: “I will surely fill up Hell with jinn and humans all together.”
phrases.explanation: The word of your Lord is fulfilled that Hell will be filled with jinn and humans together sounds severe after the exception of mercy. Filling gathers the final population of persistent rebels across unseen and human worlds, not a quota randomly selected from the innocent. In the moral logic of the chapter, people arrive there through the records argued town by town. The sentence closes speculation with a decree whose justice earlier verses have guarded.

phrases.translation: And We relate to you ˹O Prophet˺ the stories of the messengers to reassure your heart.
phrases.explanation: All the reports of messengers are related to firm the Prophet heart gives the stories an explicit purpose near the end. Noah timber, Hud trust, Salih camel, Abraham pleading, Lot door, Shuaib scale, and Moses court become companions around Muhammad. A heart steadied by precedent can endure local rejection without calling it unprecedented. History in revelation acts as emotional and strategic education rather than a museum catalogue.

phrases.translation: And there has come to you in this ˹sûrah˺ the truth, a warning ˹to the disbelievers˺, and a reminder to the believers
phrases.explanation: In this has come truth, admonition, and reminder for believers names three effects in one cluster. Truth settles what happened and Who governs it. Admonition warns the resistant before their street becomes a report. Reminder refreshes believers who already know but grow tired in a long middle. The verse explains why a chapter can repeat similar towns without wasting words, since each repetition teaches a different pressure point.

phrases.translation: Say to those who disbelieve, “Persist in your ways; we will certainly persist in ours
phrases.explanation: Say to those who do not believe, work according to your position while we are working, repeats Shuaib closing posture in Muhammad own mouth. The phrase does not celebrate their road. It releases a fruitless argument into the evidence of ongoing conduct. Believers continue revelation, prayer, patience, and reform while opponents continue their chosen work. Two kinds of activity move toward a judgment neither side can spin.

phrases.translation: And wait! Surely we ˹too˺ are waiting.”
phrases.explanation: Wait, we too are waiting gives the exchange its final open horizon. Waiting has been Noah under mockery, Hud under threat, Shuaib before the blast, and Muhammad after hearing them all. The opponents wait for prophetic failure while believers wait for divine settling. A short command becomes the drumbeat of the chapter because time is not neutral when a counted term is running. Attention now passes from debating to watching.

phrases.translation: To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs the knowledge of what is hidden in the heavens and the earth.
phrases.explanation: To Allah belongs the unseen of heavens and earth closes every argument about timing, hidden hearts, future towns, and the exact moment of judgment. Prophets preach without owning that archive, and opponents mock without escaping it. Unseen knowledge also includes sincere deeds performed where no town Chronicler stood. The verse gathers the entire chapter into a sky and earth already known from the inside by their Maker.

phrases.translation: And to Him all matters are returned. So worship Him and put your trust in Him.
phrases.explanation: To Him every matter is returned, so worship Him and trust Him turns universal knowledge into two personal actions. Return can mean referral for decision now as well as final judgment later, and both senses steady the Prophet. Worship keeps the present straight while trust holds the future. The long sequence of towns ends not with a strategy for controlling audiences but with the same surrender each messenger practised.

phrases.translation: And your Lord is never unaware of what you do
phrases.explanation: Your Lord is not heedless of what you do gives the last line to universal awareness rather than destruction. You in the broad audience includes Prophet, believers, mockers, and later readers halfway through their own counted term. No good deed will be wasted and no inclination will be missed because the witness never looks away. A chapter of vanished towns ends by assuring the living that their present work is fully seen.
